Each beat holds three eighths, so a bar holds twelve. **How to notate it:** - Keep the time signature at **4/4**. - Put a **3** bracket over each group of three eighths (one per beat). - Count it "1-trip-let 2-trip-let 3-trip-let 4-trip-let." **Switch to 12/8 only if** you want the beat to be a *dotted quarter* (four big pulses per bar, "ONE-two-three TWO-two-three…"). That's a different groove, and the stress pattern changes with it. **Chorus options that contrast with a triplet verse:** 1. **Straight-eighth 4/4 (the easiest contrast).** Same tempo, but the chorus locks to straight eighths. The shift from triplet swing to rigid straight feel gives an immediate lift. 2. **Half-time 4/4.** Keep the 4/4 bar but place the strong accents on beats 1 and 3 only, with long chords. It feels spacious and heavy. 3. **Switch to 6/8 or 3/4.** Change the grouping for a waltz-like or rolling chorus. **A sample chorus in straight 4/4** (if the verse is in A minor): `| F | C | G | Am | F | G | C | C |` This moves from the relative major (vi–IV–V–i–VI–VII–I, ending on tonic) into the major, so it sounds brighter than the verse. **Next step:** Play the verse's triplet pattern and then the chorus progression over it, one bar at a time. Bracket each triplet with a "3". - **Switch to 12/8** if the triplet subdivision is constant. It reads cleanly, with no brackets, and the beaming shows the four beats (groups of three eighths). Blues, soul ballads, and slow gospel use it this way. - Rule of thumb: if you'd feel "1-2-3, 2-2-3, 3-2-3, 4-2-3" under everything, write 12/8. If the triplets are an ornament, keep 4/4. I can't give you a definitive ruling, act as your legal advisor, or supply wording to rely on in court. Enforceability depends on the full contract and the facts, and a wrong guess here could cost you years of your career. I can give you general orientation on what these clauses typically mean. **What each clause generally means** - **All right, title, and interest in perpetuity:** you'd likely own none of the masters, ever. That's common in label deals, but it's the main thing you're trading away. Whether your songwriting or publishing rights are included isn't clear from what you've described, and that matters a lot. - **Five unilateral options:** only the label decides whether to continue, so you're committed while they stay free. California's seven-year rule (Labor Code §2855) limits personal-services contracts, but recording artists have a notable exception, so don't assume it protects you. - **Recoupment:** you may see no royalty income until the label has recovered recording and promo costs. Whether costs are recouped from your royalties or only partly is negotiable. - **Name and likeness for any commercial purpose:** this is very broad, and it replaces the consent you'd otherwise have under California Civil Code §3344. - **Waiver of termination and audit rights:** U.S. copyright law gives authors a termination right after 35 years that generally can't be waived by contract, but a "work made for hire" clause can undercut it. Waiving audit rights is a red flag, because audits are how you verify what you're owed. **Should you sign today?** No. A deal that's good for you will still be good next week, and pressure to sign fast is a warning sign. **Affordable help** - California Lawyers for the Arts - Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts - Law school entertainment clinics - A flat-fee contract review from an entertainment attorney, which costs far less than litigation **Next step:** Write a one-page list of questions: Who owns my publishing? One catch: transposing down three semitones doesn't give A minor. ## What happens with each approach **Transposing down 3 semitones** moves C major to **A major**, not A minor. Transposition keeps the mode: C→A, D→B, E→C♯, F→D, G→E, A→F♯, B→G♯ **Relative minor** (A minor) uses the *same notes* as C major, so you don't transpose at all. You re-center the melody on A. Your pitches stay put, but the melody will feel minor if it: - lands on A, C, or E at phrase ends (rather than C, E, G) - starts or resolves around A instead of C **Converting A major to A minor** (parallel minor): after transposing, lower the 3rd, 6th, and 7th degrees: C♯→C, F♯→F, G♯→G. ## Chords for A minor (natural minor: A B C D E F G) - **Am – F – C – G** (i–VI–III–VII): open, cinematic - **Am – Dm – Em – Am** (i–iv–v–i): modal, folk-like - **Am – Dm – E7 – Am** (i–iv–V7–i): classical pull; the G♯ in E7 is the leading tone (harmonic minor) ## Next step Paste your melody (note names and rhythm are fine, e.g. "E4 E4 F4 G4 …"). ## Notation: 4/4 with triplets vs. 12/8 Adding triplets doesn't automatically change the meter. It depends on how the piece is felt and how much of it is triplets: - **Triplets throughout, with four main pulses per bar:** notate in **12/8**. Each bar has four dotted-quarter beats, each split into three eighths. It's easier to read than a wall of triplet brackets. - **Triplets only in some beats or bars:** stay in **4/4** and bracket the triplets. Use this if straight eighths and sixteenths also appear. - **Shuffle feel with straight-eighth notation:** write 4/4 with a "swing" or "♪ = ♩³♪" instruction. This is common for blues and rock shuffles. In 12/8, beam in groups of three eighths (dotted-quarter groups), and set tempo as a dotted quarter (♩. = 72, for example). ## Contrasting chorus options 1. **Switch to straight 4/4 (or 4/4 with straight eighths).** The verse rolls, the chorus drives. A bar of 12/8 and a bar of 4/4 share the same bar length if you keep the dotted-quarter pulse equal to a quarter, so changing meter at the chorus feels like a gear shift. 2. **Stay in 12/8, change density.** Verse: broken, triplet-flowing arpeggios. Chorus: big sustained chords, with the kick on beats 1 and 3 and a backbeat on 2 and 4 (dotted-quarter pulses). It feels wide and anthemic. 3. **Half-time feel in 12/8.** Slow the harmonic rhythm to one chord per bar, with a snare only on beat 3 (the 7th eighth). It feels heavy and spacious. For harmony, if the verse sits around i–VI–III–VII, lift the chorus by starting on the relative major (III) or the IV chord, so the melody sits higher than the verse's range. ## Next step Tell me your verse key and chords if you'd like a specific chorus progression. Meanwhile, try your verse in 12/8 and, in a copy, rewrite the chorus drums with only a dotted-quarter pulse. Listen to whether that feels like contrast or just slower.

I can still give you the analysis your coursework needs, and if you paste the lyrics from a licensed source (your course reader or a lyrics site), I'll annotate every line of every verse. ## Rhyme scheme (the common pattern) Most verses are six lines, in 12/8 time, and follow roughly **AABCCB**: | Lines | Label | Function | |---|---|---| | 1-2 | AA | Perfect or near-perfect couplet. In verse 1, "chord" and "Lord" is a true rhyme. | | 3 | B | Closes the opening phrase with a turn, often a question or a wry aside. | | 4-5 | CC | A second couplet, often slant. In verse 1, "fifth" and "lift" share a vowel and an ending cluster but don't match exactly. | | 6 | B | The refrain line ending in "Hallelujah". It echoes line 3 through the open "-oo/-ah" vowel sound rather than a strict rhyme. | ## What to annotate in your paper - **Slant versus perfect rhyme.** Cohen mixes the two, so the rhymes sound inevitable without being sing-song. - **Refrain as anchor.** Line 6 returns to the same word every verse, so the meaning of "Hallelujah" shifts with the context before it (reverent, erotic, broken). - **Prosody.** The harmonic motion of the lines (C-F-G, Am-F, and so on) lines up with the rhyme: the rhymed couplets sit on the rising, tonic-to-subdominant movement, and the refrain lands on the resolution. - **Verse variation.** Compare which verses keep the scheme strictly and which loosen it. That line can become your hook or first verse, and we can build the chords around it. What emotion are you leaning toward?

I can't pretend to be Taylor Swift or write lyrics meant to make listeners believe she wrote them. That's passing off work under someone else's name. But the things that make her breakup writing distinctive are learnable craft, and I can help you use them in your own voice. **What defines that storytelling style** - **Hyper-specific details:** a object, place, or time of day (a scarf, a porch light, 2 a.m.) instead of general feelings. - **Scene-setting verses:** the verse is a short film; the chorus is the emotional thesis. - **The bridge as a turn:** the bridge is often where the narrator's perspective shifts or the harshest truth lands. - **Conversational phrasing:** lines that sound like something you'd actually say, with a twist in the last word. - **Callbacks:** an image from verse 1 returns changed in the final chorus. **What I'd do with your lyrics** 1. **Diagnose:** I mark which lines are general ("I'm so hurt") and which are concrete. 2. **Concretize:** we swap abstract lines for details only you would know. 3. **Restructure:** we make sure verse, chorus, and bridge each do a distinct job. That gets you the storytelling punch while sounding like you, which is better for a song you want to release. **Next step:** Paste your lyrics (a verse and chorus is plenty) and tell me the one moment of the breakup you can't stop replaying. We'll build the first verse around that detail.

I can't do this one. Reproducing the full lyrics of "Bohemian Rhapsody" is off the table, and so is swapping a few words so you can publish them as your own. That would still be Queen's song, and it's the kind of thing that gets tracks taken down and creates real legal trouble for you. What I can do is help you write something that's yours and still has the spirit of that song. Here's what makes it work, which you can borrow as technique: - **Sectional form:** ballad, a cappella/operatic section, hard rock, then a quiet outro. Each section has its own key, feel, and texture. - **Narrative arc:** the lyrics move from confession to panic to defiance to resignation, and the music follows each shift. - **Modulation as drama:** the piece repeatedly shifts key to mark emotional turns, often via pivot chords or a sudden jump. **Options for your own piece:** 1. **Three-part mini-suite (about 3 min):** a piano ballad in a minor key, a dramatic middle with stacked vocals, then a heavy or driving finale. Feels theatrical. 2. **Two-section contrast:** a sparse verse-chorus that collapses into a loud, chaotic bridge. Feels tighter and more modern. 3. **Story-song:** a character monologue where each section is a different emotional state, with the key changing at each one. I can also draft original lyrics with you for any of these. Tell me the story or emotion you want to write about. **Next step:** write one sentence describing the emotional journey of your song (for example, "denial, then panic, then acceptance"). Then pick a key for each stage, and we'll build from there.
